facts.F1: A K-class problem is split into K(K-1)/2 two-class problems; one (potentially small) neural network per pair of classes, trained only on the data of those two classes.
facts.F2: Each pairwise network's output is turned into a probability by class-conditional density estimation on its linear output (Gaussian fits in the application) plus Bayes' rule.
facts.F3: The pairwise probabilities are combined into posterior class probabilities with a closed-form formula: P(class i | x) = 1 / (sum over j != i of 1/P_ij - (K-2)).
facts.F4: It contrasts with an earlier method that uses only K-1 pairwise probabilities, whose quality depends critically on choosing that subset.
facts.F5: Application: pre-segmented cursive handwritten characters from real French postal checks; 27 classes; 351 single-neuron pairwise classifiers; 10x24-pixel inputs.
facts.F6: About 55,000 characters split into training (20,000), validation (20,000) and test (15,000) sets.
facts.F7: Results: the pairwise classifier reaches 48.9% (equal priors) / 52.2% (true priors) top-1; a Softmax-trained MLP is the most accurate (54.9% / 61.9%) - the pairwise classifier does NOT beat the best MLP on recognition rate.
facts.F8: Advantages claimed: training over an order of magnitude faster than MLPs, classes can be added/modified without retraining all pairwise classifiers, and more insight into the problem.
facts.F9: The classifier is part of a deployed check-reading system (83.3% of words found in first position; 80% of checks recognized at 1% error).
